body.text: Which historic synagogues (Neve Shalom, Ahrida, Ashkenazi, Quincentennial Museum) can visitors tour?

Visitors can tour the [Quincentennial Foundation Museum of Turkish Jews](https://www.muze500.com/) inside the Neve Shalom complex in Galata, the 15th-century Ahrida Synagogue in Balat, and the 1900 Ashkenazi Synagogue near Karaköy. Each site operates under distinct visiting windows, Saturday Shabbat closures, and community security checks, so verifying hours in advance is essential.

Located on Büyük Hendek Caddesi in Galata, the [Quincentennial Foundation Museum of Turkish Jews](https://www.muze500.com/) relocated from the former Zülfaris Synagogue to the Neve Shalom complex in December 2015. Across three floors, its galleries document 2,600 years of Jewish life in Anatolia, from Byzantine Romaniote communities and the 1492 Sephardic arrival to modern Republican history. A glass-partitioned midrash hall connects directly to Neve Shalom's main sanctuary. Published hours run Sunday through Thursday from 10:00 to 17:00 and Friday from 10:00 to 13:00, with last entry 45 minutes before closing and full closures on Saturdays and religious or national holidays.

In Balat along the Golden Horn, Ahrida Synagogue—founded by Romaniote Jews from Ohrid in the early 15th century—is known for its boat-shaped tevah (reading platform). Back in Galata, the Austro-Hungarian-built Ashkenazi Synagogue on Yüksek Kaldırım Caddesi remains Istanbul's sole active Ashkenazi congregation open to pre-approved weekday visitors.

body.text: Why is advance passport registration required before visiting synagogues?

Advance passport registration protects active Turkish Jewish congregations following historical security incidents, including the 1986 and 2003 attacks on Neve Shalom. Community security offices screen visitor lists ahead of entry, cross-checking original physical passports at the door against pre-approved names before unlocking sanctuary gates.

Security procedures are routine, polite, and non-negotiable across Istanbul and İzmir. Unlike public state museums, most Turkish synagogues are privately maintained by local foundations rather than the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. Unannounced walk-ups at Balat's Ahrida or Yanbol synagogues are routinely turned away, even when doors appear staffed.

items: Carry your original physical passport (photocopies and phone photos are generally declined at security gates).
Dress modestly with covered shoulders and knees; men should expect to wear a kippah provided at the entrance.
Avoid scheduling visits on Saturdays (Shabbat), Friday afternoons, or Jewish and Turkish public holidays.
Confirm photography restrictions on site—flash and interior sanctuary photography are often prohibited.
Allow 15–20 extra minutes per stop for bag screening and ID verification.

body.text: What Sephardic heritage exists in İzmir's Kemeraltı Havra Sokağı?

İzmir's [Havra Sokağı](https://www.izmirjh.com/en/ana-sayfa/birinci-yahudi-mahallesi/havra-sokagi/) ("Synagogue Street") inside the historic Kemeraltı Bazaar preserves one of the Mediterranean's densest clusters of 17th- and 19th-century Sephardic synagogues. Nine historic sanctuaries stand within walking distance of one another, reflecting the commercial community that thrived after Iberian exiles settled along the Aegean coast.

Restored and documented through the EU-supported [İzmir Jewish Heritage Project](https://izmirjh.com/ana-sayfa/birinci-yahudi-mahallesi/sinagoglar/), the district features distinct architectural landmarks including Bikur Holim, Etz Hayim, Shalom (Aydınlı), Algazi, Sinyora (Giveret), and the Portugal Synagogue. Several interiors display the traditional central tevah framed by four columns—a spatial layout characteristic of early Ottoman Sephardic architecture. Beyond Kemeraltı, the 1907 Karataş Asansör (historic public elevator), built by Jewish businessman Nesim Levi Bayraklıoğlu to connect the coastal road to the upper Karataş neighborhood, remains a defining civic monument. Researchers and heritage travelers can also consult the [Jewish Heritage Europe Turkey directory](https://jewish-heritage-europe.eu/turkey/heritage-heritage-sites/) for broader Anatolian context, including ancient Sardis.

faq.q: Can I visit the Quincentennial Foundation Museum of Turkish Jews without booking weeks ahead?
faq.a: Yes. Individual travelers can usually enter the museum in Galata during published Sunday–Friday hours by presenting an original passport or national ID at the security desk, though checking for holiday closures beforehand is wise.

faq.q: Are Istanbul and İzmir synagogues open on Saturdays?
faq.a: No. Tourist visits are not permitted on Saturdays (Shabbat), Friday afternoons, or major Jewish and Turkish public holidays. Weekday mornings between Monday and Thursday offer the widest access window.

faq.q: Is Ahrida Synagogue in Balat open to walk-in visitors?
faq.a: No. Ahrida Synagogue requires advance written permission and passport clearance through official Istanbul Jewish community channels before arrival.

faq.q: How much time should I allocate for Istanbul's Jewish heritage sites?
faq.a: Plan one full weekday (6–7 hours) to combine Galata (Quincentennial Museum, Neve Shalom, Ashkenazi Synagogue, Kamondo Steps) with Balat (Ahrida Synagogue and historic streets) without rushing security checks.

faq.q: Can I combine İzmir's Havra Sokağı with ancient Sardis?
faq.a: Yes. Many travelers spend a morning walking Kemeraltı's Havra Sokağı and Karataş Asansör, then dedicate a separate day trip (roughly 90 minutes east of İzmir) to the monumental 4th-century CE synagogue ruins at Sardis.

faq.q: Do I need to send my passport copy in my first enquiry to Itinerary of Türkiye?
faq.a: No. Never send passport scans, ID documents, medical or financial records, or payment information in an initial enquiry; security registration is handled later through official community channels once dates are confirmed.
